newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean deficit swells, strikes blamed.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean deficit swells, strikes blamed.

text.p: South Korea on Tuesday blamed a month of strikes for a hefty 80 percent leap in the country's current account deficit in January.
South Korea ran a $3.09 billion current account deficit in January, almost double the $1.72 billion shortfall a year earlier, the central Bank of Korea said.
The figures followed trade account data released on Monday which analysts said showed signs of an emerging recovery in the country's terms of trade.

"January results reflected damage from the labour strikes. But the February figures suggest the trading performance will recover from later this year as we have forecast," said Lee Youn-ho, president of the LG Economic Research Institute.
On Monday the country posted a customs-cleared trade deficit of $2.1 billion for February, a slight increase from a $1.6 billion shortfall in the same 1996 month.
The current account measures foreign trade of goods and services plus transfers, while the trade account consists of goods and services on a customs-cleared basis.

The central bank said last month's strikes at key export industries, including carmakers, contributed to a trade deficit in January of $2.25 billion, a situation which drove open the current account deficit.
Work stoppages idled the nation's major manufacturing sectors in January after a new labour law, designed to create a more flexible labour market, was rammed through parliament in December.
The law was sent back to parliament for fresh debate between ruling and opposition parties after President Kim Young-sam ordered a revision of the legislation.
Automobile exports, hardest hit by the strikes, fell 42.9 percent year-on-year in January to $440 million on a customs-cleared basis.
A continued slump in semiconductor exports as a result of weak international prices for dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips also hampered the trade account.
Electronics exports fell 14.9 percent to $1.96 billion in January, compared with growth of 43.2 percent a year earlier.
"I expect damage from the weak DRAM prices to wane from the second half when year-on-year price differences will be much smaller than in the first half," said Lee.
Analysts also expected impact on South Korean exporters from the steep slide of the Japanese yen against the U.S. dollar to ease as the conversion rate stabilised.
The weak yen has made the price of Japanese goods sold abroad cheaper when compared with South Korean goods.
The yen lost about seven percent in the first two months of this year to around 125 yen per dollar from around 115 yen at the end of last year.
South Korea's won also lost to the U.S. dollar but the pace has been much slower than the Japanese yen.
South Korea's Finance and Economy Ministry has forecast this year's current account deficit at about $18 billion, compared with a $23.72 billion shortfall in 1996.
